taxonomy.note: Accepted species; two accepted varieties preserved in review while learner remains species-level.
accepted_infraspecifics: Ilex decidua var. mulleri Edwin ex T.R.Dudley

evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Ilex decidua and lists Texas in its native range.
Hays County — the project Hays County native-source list includes I. decidua, and Purola Preserve separately documents naturally occurring possumhaw.

Travis County — Travis County's Pace Bend Park plant inventory documents deciduous holly as a characteristic understory shrub in native woodland, and Texas Wildbuds documents natural central-Texas material.
Williamson County — the University of Texas Plant Resources Center provides a dedicated Williamson County treatment and includes I. decidua in the county flora.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Possumhaw is widely used in landscaping, so county decisions rely on native-flora/park/herbarium context rather than ornamental plantings. Kew recognizes var. decidua and var. mulleri; B017 stays species-level.

morphology.look_here_first: First ask whether the holly is deciduous: possumhaw drops its leaves and leaves dense red/orange drupes exposed along pale gray twigs in winter. In leaf, its blades are larger and thinner than yaupon and usually elliptic to obovate with shallow crenate teeth.
diagnostic_traits: deciduous shrub or small tree, often with pale gray twiggy branches
leaves alternate, simple, thin-textured, elliptic to obovate/spatulate
leaf margin shallowly crenate to crenate-serrate, not stiffly spiny
small inconspicuous white flowers are axillary; plants are primarily dioecious
female plants bear red to orange-red drupes in clusters along twigs
fruits commonly persist after leaf drop, making winter fruiting twigs highly diagnostic
tiny stipules may be present at petiole bases in detailed regional treatments
typically associated with moist woods, creek bottoms, floodplains and low areas

confusers.separator: Yaupon is evergreen with much smaller leathery leaves and fine crenate teeth; possumhaw is deciduous with larger thinner leaves and famously bare fruit-covered twigs in winter.
American holly is an evergreen tree with much larger thick leaves bearing sharp spine-tipped teeth; possumhaw leaves are thinner, non-spiny, and deciduous.
Winterberry is also deciduous and red-fruited but is primarily an eastern/northern wetland species; use verified range plus leaf/fruiting details before applying the name in Texas.

installation_guardrail: Do not install until Calvin explicitly approves B017 pass taxa.
